result: Perivascular cells in the mouse ear dermis become visible after HMw dextran injection, are mostly sessile, constantly uptake intravascular dextran, and extend protrusions into vessel lumens that flap with blood flow and contact circulating cells.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by intravital imaging data (Figure 1A, Videos 1-4), dextran pulse-chase experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and vivotag imaging (Figure 1B). The dynamic behavior of protrusions is documented through video microscopy showing flapping motion and cell contact.

result: The dextran+ perivascular cells are predominantly macrophages, with 96.67% ± 1.02% being CD45+, 90.41% ± 2.06% of CD45+ cells being CD64+ macrophages, representing 41.28% ± 5.66% of total skin macrophages, and expressing markers CD45+ F4/80high CD11c- CD11b+ or CD64+ and CD68+.
evaluation: Claims C6-C10 are supported by flow cytometry data from skin single-cell suspensions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). The quantitative measurements and phenotypic characterization are consistent across multiple techniques.

result: Skin macrophages are preferentially localized around dermal blood microvessels rather than lymphatics, mostly apposed to capillaries and venules, possibly due to the dense smooth muscle layer around arterioles preventing access.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by mesoscopic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Video 5) and microscopy observations. However, C13 is speculative reasoning without direct experimental evidence, though the overall spatial distribution pattern is well-documented.

result: Endothelial cells did not detectably capture dextran under experimental conditions, ruling out transcytosis as a mechanism for making intravascular dextran accessible to perivascular macrophages.
evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by FACS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) demonstrating lack of dextran uptake by CD31+ endothelial cells. The inference that transcytosis is not the mechanism is logically sound based on this negative result.

result: Dextran+ macrophages embrace vessels from outside the pericyte sheath, with protrusions extending across the basement membrane and between pericytes to reach the endothelial wall, aligning with and inserting through endothelial intercellular junctions.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19 are well-supported by whole-mount immunofluorescence staining (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), intravital microscopy with anti-CD31 staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 6), and orthogonal sectioning analysis (Figure 2B). Multiple imaging modalities converge on the same conclusion.

result: TRITC-dextran uptake was minimal in VE-cadherin-α-catenin knock-in mice with stabilized endothelial junctions, demonstrating that macrophages access the vascular lumen by crossing endothelial junctions via a paracellular route, not a transcellular route.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are supported by quantitative data comparing wild-type and VE-cadherin-α-catenin mice (Figure 2C) and citation to the characterization of this mouse model (Schulte et al., 2011). The genetic model provides strong evidence for the paracellular mechanism by showing that stabilized junctions restrict macrophage access.

result: The capture of dextran by skin myeloid cells is mediated by the mannose receptor (CD206), enabling selective in vivo staining of intraluminal protrusions of dermal perivascular macrophages, confirming the existence of these hitherto unidentified macrophages in homeostatic conditions.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by citation to previous work (Wollenberg et al., 2002) and experimental data showing in vivo staining with anti-CD206 (Figure 2D). The collective evidence from multiple experiments establishes the existence of this macrophage population.

result: Dextran+ dermal macrophages did not express GFP in chimeric animals reconstituted with β-actin-GFP+ hematopoietic progenitors, were not replaced by BM-derived macrophages after irradiation, and persisted 7 days after lethal γ-irradiation, indicating they are a specialized radio-resistant subset.
evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by imaging and flow cytometry data from chimeric mice (Figure 3A, Video 7) and imaging after irradiation without reconstitution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The lack of GFP expression in donor-derived cells provides strong evidence for radio-resistance.

result: In chimeric mice, hematopoietic reconstitution was complete in blood and lymphoid organs after 12 weeks, but skin myeloid subsets showed higher host contribution. Host radio-resistant CD45.2+ macrophages efficiently captured dextran and were positioned around microvessels, confirmed in parabiotic mice where only host macrophages captured intraluminal dextran.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37 are supported by flow cytometry analysis of chimerism in different organs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D), imaging and flow cytometry of dextran uptake in chimeric mice (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and parabiosis experiments (Figure 3C). Multiple experimental approaches converge on the same conclusion.

result: While radio-resistant dendritic cells in skin have been previously reported, radio-resistant dermal macrophages (STREAMs) have remained elusive until this study. STREAMs coexist with radio-sensitive macrophages in steady state, and may have a human homolog.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by citations to previous work (Bogunovic et al., 2006; Merad et al., 2002) and the experimental evidence from chimerism and parabiosis experiments. C41 is speculative but reasonably grounded in citation to Haniffa et al., 2009.

result: STREAMs are maintained locally in the skin throughout adult life independently of circulatory precursors, while radio-sensitive macrophages are renewed from blood in steady state and replaced by donor BM progenitors after genotoxic insult, extending previous knowledge on tissue-resident macrophages.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by chimerism, parabiosis, and fate mapping experimental data, and citations to previous work (Hashimoto et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013). The inference about local maintenance is well-supported by the collective evidence.

result: UV irradiation had a negative effect on the survival and renewal of host compared to donor macrophages in chimeric mice, indicating radio-resistant macrophages are UV-sensitive. However, they do not express langerin and are distinguishable from Langerhans cells.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by flow cytometry data comparing host and donor macrophages after UV irradiation (Figure 5A) and imaging data showing lack of langerin expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The differential sensitivity to UV versus γ-irradiation is well-documented.

result: Host radio-resistant macrophages lack self-renewal capacity in steady-state as shown by Ki-67 staining, have slower turnover than donor macrophages and Langerhans cells as shown by BrdU incorporation, and are outcompeted over time by BM-derived macrophages, suggesting they are long-lived cells originating from an in situ proliferating progenitor.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by Ki-67 staining data (Figure 5B), BrdU incorporation data (Figure 5C), longitudinal flow cytometry (Figure 5D), and clodronate depletion/recovery experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The inference about origin from a proliferating progenitor is well-supported by the collective evidence.

result: Skin-resident macrophages lack pluripotent potential in steady-state, but YFP+ macrophages appear in Bmi1 reporter mice 5 days after tamoxifen, suggesting derivation from a Bmi1+ progenitor. YFP+ macrophage generation increases after clodronate depletion, and YFP+ dextran+ macrophages exist in chimeric mice lacking tamoxifen-inducible BM cells, confirming in situ generation from a skin progenitor independent of BM.
evaluation: Claims C52-C59 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), flow cytometry from Bmi1 reporter mice (Figure 5E), microscopy (Figure 5F), flow cytometry from chimeric Bmi1 mice (Figure 5G-H), and intravital imaging (Figure 5I). The fate mapping experiments provide strong evidence for the extramedullary origin.

result: Two distinct skin-resident macrophage pools coexist in homeostasis based on their differential capacity to uptake circulating macromolecules, sensitivity to γ-irradiation, and progenitor source.
evaluation: Claim C60 is a summary inference supported by the collective experimental evidence from chimerism, parabiosis, fate mapping, and functional studies presented throughout the manuscript.

result: Both host and donor macrophage subsets share many markers (F4/80high, CD11b+, Ly6C, CD115, CD68, CD64-MertK, CD11c-, Ly6G-, Tie-2, CD40, CD70, MHC-I), but host macrophages show higher CD86 and CD206, while donor macrophages show higher MHC-II. However, the broad range of expression precludes using these markers to accurately dissect heterogeneity.
evaluation: Claims C61-C68 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and citation to Gautier et al., 2012. The phenotypic characterization is comprehensive, and the limitation regarding marker overlap is appropriately acknowledged.

result: RNA-Seq analysis of 17,741 genes found significant differences in 744 genes (135 protein coding with consistent expression). GSEA showed 36 Kegg pathways upregulated in host macrophages versus 149 in donor macrophages, confirming striking metabolic differences between the two populations.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by RNA-Seq data analysis (Figure 6B-C, Supplementary file 1) and GSEA results (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 2). The transcriptional profiling is comprehensive and statistically sound.

result: Host radio-resistant macrophages display a metabolic gene profile based on fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation with elevated mitochondrial function, while donor BM-derived macrophages show a glycolytic profile. Both subsets contain comparable mitochondria per cell. These profiles mirror the metabolic reprogramming of anti-inflammatory (M2) and pro-inflammatory (M1) macrophages, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by GSEA analysis of metabolic pathways and flow cytometry data showing mitochondrial function (MitoTracker) and content (Tomm20) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B). The comparison to M1/M2 polarization is supported by citation to Galvan-Pena and O'Neill, 2014.

result: Donor-derived macrophages show increased expression of H2-Eb1, Ccr2, Il1β, Il6, and Il10 (pro-inflammatory cytokines), while host macrophages show upregulated Cd86, Il15, and Hmox, with elevated protein expression of heme oxygenase-1, arginase I, and higher TGF-β production in resting conditions.
evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 7A), immunostaining (Figure 7B), and ELISA (Figure 7C), with citation to Rodriguez-Prados et al., 2010 for the pro-inflammatory role of the cytokines. The validation of RNA-Seq findings at the protein level strengthens the conclusions.

result: Dermal macrophages expressing low MHC-II (never exposed to γ-irradiation) and remaining macrophages 7 days after lethal γ-irradiation lack upregulation of proinflammatory genes, while MHC-IIhigh macrophages possess a pro-inflammatory profile. Prior irradiation did not alter immune gene expression profiles. The radio-resistant subset is skewed towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype in steady-state and is termed STREAMs (Skin Transendothelial Radio-resistant Anti-inflammatory Macrophages).
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) comparing different macrophage populations. The inference that irradiation did not alter profiles is supported by comparison of irradiated and non-irradiated animals. The naming of STREAMs is based on the collective characteristics identified.

result: Both macrophage subsets express LPS receptors, but pro-inflammatory macrophages produce substantial CCL4, CCL5, CXCL1, TNF-α, and IL-6 in response to LPS, while anti-inflammatory macrophages do not produce significant amounts of these mediators. However, anti-inflammatory macrophages produce IL-10 in response to IL-4, suggesting they are refractory to pro-inflammatory challenges but responsive to anti-inflammatory stimuli, indicating functional commitment in steady-state.
evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by flow cytometry showing receptor expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), multiplex cytokine analysis (Figure 7D), and ELISA (Figure 7E). The differential responses to LPS versus IL-4 provide strong evidence for functional specialization and lack of plasticity.

result: OVA fluospheres injected i.v. are specifically captured by skin macrophages, a process abrogated by clodronate depletion. The capturing macrophages are dextran+ in wild-type animals and radio-resistant in chimeric mice. Capture by skin STREAMs is low compared to splenic macrophages but increases in γ-irradiated and splenectomized animals.
evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 8A-B, 8D-E), intravital imaging (Figure 8C, Videos 8-9), and comparison with splenic macrophages (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B). The experiments demonstrate the specific ability of STREAMs to capture blood-borne nanoparticles.

result: DT-OVA-NP treatment depleted preferentially STREAMs while preserving most other skin macrophages, providing a method for selective depletion.
evaluation: Claim C99 is supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) showing selective depletion of the anti-inflammatory subset. This represents a key methodological advance enabling functional studies.

result: Macrophage depletion with DT-OVA-NP (administered 1 day before and 2 days after wounding) was associated with significant delay in healing at mid-stage (day 5), with marked reduction in granulation tissue formation, reduced angiogenesis, and delayed re-epithelialization.
evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by wound area measurements (Figure 9B) and histological analysis (Figure 9C-D). The experimental design with multiple doses and mid-stage analysis is appropriate for assessing the role of macrophages in wound healing.

result: Administration of DT-OVA-NP 2 days after wounding (after the initial inflammatory phase) resulted in clear defects in collagen deposition and disordered myofibroblast distribution, indicating STREAMs play a prominent role in orchestrating tissue remodeling and repair.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by Masson trichrome staining (Figure 10A) and α-SMA staining (Figure 10B). The timing of depletion after the inflammatory phase strengthens the conclusion about the specific role in tissue remodeling.

result: No substantial differences were observed in wound closure, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast distribution in Ccr2-/- mice or Ccr2-/-/Ccr2+/+ chimeras compared to controls, strengthening the idea of a selective role for STREAMs in tissue repair.
evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are supported by wound healing data in Ccr2-/- mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C-D) and chimeric mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1F-G). The lack of defects in these models where radio-sensitive macrophages are depleted/prevented from repopulating provides strong evidence for the specific role of STREAMs.

result: STREAMs capture blood-borne macromolecules by extending protrusions into the vascular lumen at steady-state, are committed to anti-inflammatory functions lacking plasticity to be reprogrammed by pro-inflammatory stimuli, and their selective depletion highlights their function in tissue repair and remodeling.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are summary statements supported by the collective experimental evidence from imaging, chimerism, transcriptional profiling, functional assays, and wound healing experiments presented throughout the manuscript.

result: Specialized macrophage subtypes in lymph nodes and liver can traverse fenestrated sinusoids to capture antigens, dendritic cells extend transepithelial projections in airways and gut, some specialized dendritic cells have been redefined as macrophages, CX3CR1+ myeloid cells in CNS can access vasculature, and mast cells capture blood-borne IgE by unknown mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by citations to previous work establishing this knowledge in the literature. These claims provide context for the novelty of the current findings.

result: STREAMs are unique in traversing endothelial junctions of non-fenestrated dermal vasculature under homeostatic conditions via a paracellular route. Unlike subcapsular sinus macrophages that retain antigens on their surface, STREAMs internalize particulate antigens and might play a role in cross-presentation to tissue-resident memory CD8+ T cells.
evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are well-supported by the experimental data using VE-cadherin-α-catenin mice and comparison with other macrophage types. However, C119 regarding cross-presentation is speculative without direct experimental evidence. The potential role in antigen presentation requires further investigation.

result: Radio-resistant dendritic cells in skin have been previously reported, and the current results concur with previous studies showing dual origin for skin macrophages (prenatally-derived CCR2-independent and postnatal BM-derived CCR2-dependent), with the prenatal subset displaced by the BM-derived subset with age. This dual origin has also been observed in heart.
evaluation: Claims C120-C123 are supported by citations to previous work (Bogunovic et al., 2006; Merad et al., 2002; Jakubzick et al., 2013; Tamoutounour et al., 2013; Molawi et al., 2014) and the current experimental data showing changes in macrophage composition over time.

result: Yolk sac-derived Myb-independent F4/80bright macrophages might correspond to the developmental precursor for STREAMs, while c-Myb dependent fetal liver monocytes might be precursors of radiosensitive macrophages.
evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are speculative inferences based on citations to Schulz et al., 2012 and Hoeffel et al., 2015. While the speculation is reasonable given the current findings and previous literature, direct experimental evidence linking these developmental precursors to the adult macrophage subsets is lacking.

result: Previous classifications of skin macrophages based on phenotypic markers identified heterogeneity but not related to radio-sensitivity. MHC-II expression cannot precisely discriminate the two subsets with distinct radio-sensitivity, polarization profiles, and functions. The classification criteria used in this work allows better resolution of skin macrophage subsets.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by flow cytometry data showing overlapping MHC-II expression (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and reference to previous classification schemes. The limitation of phenotypic markers and the advantage of the functional/ontogeny-based classification are well-demonstrated.

result: Metabolic adaptation is key in macrophage activation. The current study along with others showing polarized macrophages in steady state in various tissues helps reformulate the paradigm that macrophage specialization arises mainly from external stimuli. In pancreas, anatomical localization imprints distinct features (M1 in islets, M2 in stroma), but in skin, pro- and anti-inflammatory macrophages coexist in the same areas. STREAMs' access to intravascular milieu might provide selective signals maintaining their phenotype, though environmental control of macrophage identity remains essential.
evaluation: Claims C129-C137 are supported by citations to multiple studies (Martinez et al., 2013; Calderon et al., 2015; DeFalco et al., 2014; Pinto et al., 2012; Gordon and Pluddemann, 2013; Sica and Mantovani, 2012; Gosselin et al., 2014; Lavin et al., 2014; Abtin et al., 2014) and the current findings. The discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within the broader literature on macrophage polarization and tissue-specific programming.

result: Preferential depletion of anti-inflammatory STREAMs has deleterious impact in wounded skin, indicating they orchestrate pro-reparative M2 functions. Conversely, wound closure was unaffected in Ccr2-/- animals and chimeric Ccr2-/-/Ccr2+/+ mice, indicating infiltrating monocytes and radiosensitive macrophages are mostly dispensable for the reparative phase. The coexistence of non-redundant macrophage subsets highlights the need for equilibrium to preserve skin fitness, with potential clinical significance.
evaluation: Claims C138-C142 are supported by wound healing data with DT-OVA-NP (Figures 9-10), Ccr2-/- mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C-D), and chimeric mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1F-G), with citations to Das et al., 2015 and Willenborg et al., 2012. C143 is speculative about clinical implications but reasonably grounded in the findings. The functional specialization and non-redundancy are well-demonstrated.
